entries.age_10: Think of a company as a giant pizza. A share is one slice. If you own a slice, you own a tiny piece of that company. If the company does well, people want slices more, so your slice becomes worth more.
entries.age_15: A share is a small piece of ownership in a company. Companies sell shares to raise money. People buy them hoping the company grows, so the share price goes up, and sometimes to get a part of the profits, called dividends.
entries.adult: A share is a unit of equity ownership in a listed company. Its market price is whatever buyers and sellers agree on at a given moment, driven by expectations of future earnings, interest rates, and overall market sentiment.
entries.in_this_app: Every company you search for in this app is a stock listed on India's National Stock Exchange (NSE).

entries.age_10: The NSE is like a huge market where people buy and sell shares instead of fruits and vegetables. Every company there has a short nickname, like RELIANCE or TCS. That nickname is called a ticker.
entries.age_15: The National Stock Exchange of India (NSE), based in Mumbai, is India's largest stock exchange. A ticker is the short code for a company's shares. Yahoo Finance adds '.NS' to show it is the NSE listing, so Reliance becomes RELIANCE.NS. India's other big exchange is the BSE, which uses '.BO'.
entries.adult: NSE is India's largest exchange by trading volume; BSE is the older exchange. Many companies are listed on both. Ticker suffixes (.NS, .BO) identify the listing for data providers like Yahoo Finance.
entries.in_this_app: You can type a normal company name like 'Tata Motors' and the app finds the right NSE ticker for you.

entries.age_10: The stock market is like a shop with fixed opening hours. It is open on weekdays during the day. When it is closed, prices don't change, so the app shows you the last price from when the shop closed.
entries.age_15: The NSE's regular trading session runs from 9:15 AM to 3:30 PM Indian time, Monday to Friday, except on exchange holidays. Outside these hours no regular trading happens, so the latest price is the previous closing price.
entries.adult: NSE's normal market session is 9:15 AM to 3:30 PM IST on trading days, with a pre-open session before 9:15. Outside market hours, quoted prices are the last close.
entries.in_this_app: When the market is closed, the app shows the last closing price and tells you when the market opens next.

entries.age_10: The 'last close' is the price a share had when the market shut for the day. The small red or green number tells you if it went up (green) or down (red) compared with the day before.
entries.age_15: The closing price is the final price of the trading day. The change shows how much it rose or fell compared with the previous day's close, both in rupees and as a percentage.
entries.adult: The close is the official end-of-day price. Daily change is measured against the previous close. Closing prices are the standard input for most indicators and backtests.
entries.in_this_app: The big price at the top is the last close, with the change versus the previous close just below it.

entries.age_10: Each little bar on the chart is one day. Green means the price went up that day, red means it went down. The thin lines sticking out show the highest and lowest the price reached that day.
entries.age_15: A candlestick shows four prices for one day: open, close, high and low. The thick part (body) is between the open and the close. It is green if the price closed higher than it opened and red if lower. The thin lines (wicks) show the day's high and low.
entries.adult: Candlesticks show the open, high, low and close (OHLC) for each period. A long body shows a strong move from open to close; long wicks show prices that were tried and pushed back. Technicians study candle patterns, ideally together with trend and support/resistance rather than alone.
entries.in_this_app: The price history chart shows one candle per trading day. Hover over a candle to see that day's exact prices.

entries.age_10: Paper trading is like playing a shop game with toy money. You can buy and sell real companies' shares at real prices, but no real money is used, so you can learn without losing anything.
entries.age_15: Paper trading means practising buying and selling stocks with virtual money. Prices are real, so you see what would have happened, but nothing is actually bought and no real money can be won or lost.
entries.adult: Paper trading simulates order execution at market prices without capital at risk. It is useful for learning and testing discipline, though it can't fully reproduce real-world factors like slippage, liquidity and the emotional pressure of real money.
entries.in_this_app: You choose a starting amount of virtual money (like Rs 1,00,000) and can buy and sell any stock in the app. Your portfolio is saved under your name.

entries.age_10: Your portfolio is your collection of shares, like a collection of cards. It shows which companies you own and how many pieces of each.
entries.age_15: A portfolio is all the investments a person owns, plus their cash. Looking at it as a whole shows your total value and whether you are making or losing money overall.
entries.adult: A portfolio is the full set of holdings and cash. What matters is not just each position's performance but how they combine: overall return, risk, diversification and correlation between holdings.
entries.in_this_app: The paper trading tab shows your cash, the shares you hold, their current value and your total profit or loss.

entries.age_10: Buying means using your money to get shares. Selling means giving your shares back to the market and getting money in return. You make money if you sell for more than you paid.
entries.age_15: When you buy, money leaves your cash balance and you get shares at the current price. When you sell, the shares are exchanged back for cash at the current price. Profit or loss depends on the difference between your buying and selling price.
entries.adult: Orders here execute at the latest available price, similar to a market order. Real markets also involve bid-ask spreads, slippage and transaction charges, which reduce returns.
entries.in_this_app: Pick a stock, enter how many shares, and press Buy or Sell. You can only sell shares you own.

entries.age_10: If you buy one sticker for Rs 10 and another for Rs 20, on average each one cost you Rs 15. The app does the same with shares.
entries.age_15: If you buy the same stock several times at different prices, your average price is the total amount you spent divided by the total number of shares. Your profit or loss is measured against this average.
entries.adult: Weighted average cost = total cost of all purchases / total shares held. Selling part of a holding doesn't change the average cost of the remaining shares.
entries.in_this_app: Your holdings table shows the average price you paid for each stock.

entries.age_10: Profit means you have more money than you started with. Loss means you have less. If your shares go up in price, you are in profit, but it only becomes 'real' when you sell.
entries.age_15: Unrealised P&L is the gain or loss on shares you still hold, based on today's price. Realised P&L is the gain or loss locked in when you actually sell. The percentage shows it relative to what you paid.
entries.adult: Unrealised P&L = (current price - average cost) x quantity. Realised P&L is crystallised on sale. In real investing, realised gains may attract capital gains tax.
entries.in_this_app: The paper trading tab shows your overall profit or loss and the P&L for each stock you hold.

entries.age_10: Imagine averaging your last 50 test marks. One bad test doesn't change the average much, so it shows how you are really doing. A moving average does this for a stock's price, so you can see its real direction instead of the daily ups and downs.
entries.age_15: A moving average is the average closing price over the last few days, recalculated every day. The 50-day average shows the medium-term direction and the 200-day shows the long-term direction. When the price is above them, the trend is usually up; when below, usually down.
entries.adult: Simple moving averages smooth out price noise and act as trend filters. They lag the price by design. The 200-day average is the most widely watched long-term trend line, often used to separate healthy uptrends from weak phases.
entries.in_this_app: The two lines on the price chart are the 50-day and 200-day moving averages.

entries.age_10: When the faster average line (50-day) climbs above the slower one (200-day), people call it a 'golden cross', a hint that things may be getting better. When it falls below, it's a 'death cross', a hint things may be getting worse.
entries.age_15: A golden cross is when the 50-day moving average rises above the 200-day, suggesting a shift to an uptrend. A death cross is the opposite. They are popular signals, but they come late because averages lag the price.
entries.adult: 50/200-day crossovers are classic trend-change signals. They lag the price and give false signals (whipsaws) when prices move sideways, so they work best as filters for the overall trend rather than precise entry signals.
entries.in_this_app: The moving-average crossover strategy in Strategy tests is based on this idea.

entries.age_10: Think of the grey band as the road the price usually drives on. Most of the time the price stays inside. When the road gets wider, the price is bouncing around a lot; when it gets narrow, things are calm, and a big move might be coming.
entries.age_15: Bollinger Bands are drawn 2 standard deviations above and below a 20-day moving average. The price stays inside the bands most of the time. Wide bands mean high volatility; narrow bands (a 'squeeze') mean low volatility, which often comes before a bigger move.
entries.adult: Bollinger Bands = 20-period SMA +/- 2 standard deviations. They adapt to volatility. Touching a band isn't a signal by itself; John Bollinger recommends combining them with other indicators, and in strong trends price can 'walk the band'.
entries.in_this_app: The grey shaded area around the price chart is the Bollinger Bands, labelled 'usual price range'.

entries.age_10: A trend is like walking up or down a hill. Uptrend: the price keeps climbing overall, even with small dips. Downtrend: it keeps sliding down. Sideways: it's walking on flat ground.
entries.age_15: A trend is the general direction of the price over time. In an uptrend, prices make higher highs and higher lows; in a downtrend, lower highs and lower lows. The app judges trend by where the price is compared with its 50-day and 200-day averages.
entries.adult: Trend identification is the foundation of technical analysis: the trend is assumed to persist until evidence shows it has reversed. Moving averages, trendlines and higher-high/higher-low structure are common tools.
entries.in_this_app: The 'Trend direction' card says whether the price is above or below its 50-day and 200-day averages.

entries.age_10: Support is like a floor where the price keeps bouncing up because lots of people want to buy there. Resistance is like a ceiling where it keeps getting pushed down because lots of people want to sell there.
entries.age_15: Support is a price level where buying has repeatedly stopped a fall. Resistance is a level where selling has repeatedly stopped a rise. When price breaks through one, it often moves strongly in that direction.
entries.adult: Support and resistance reflect concentrations of demand and supply. A broken resistance often becomes support and vice versa. They are commonly used for stop-loss placement and price targets. (This app doesn't draw these levels.)
entries.in_this_app: Not shown directly in the app, but you can often spot these levels by eye on the price chart.

entries.age_10: RSI is like a speedometer for a price. It goes from 0 to 100. Near 100, the price has been racing up very fast and might need a rest. Near 0, it has been falling fast and might bounce. But just like a fast car, it can keep going!
entries.age_15: RSI measures how strong recent gains are compared with recent losses, usually over 14 days, on a scale of 0 to 100. Above 70 is called 'overbought' (rose fast) and below 30 'oversold' (fell fast). Above 50 generally means positive momentum.
entries.adult: RSI(14) = 100 - 100/(1 + RS), where RS = average gain / average loss over 14 periods. 70/30 are conventional thresholds, but in strong trends RSI can stay overbought or oversold for long periods. Divergences between RSI and price can warn of weakening trends.
entries.in_this_app: The 'Recent strength (RSI)' card shows the current 14-day RSI with a plain-English meaning.

entries.age_10: Overbought means everyone rushed to buy, so the price ran up very fast, like a crowd running to a shop. Oversold means everyone rushed to sell. After a rush, things often calm down, but not always.
entries.age_15: Overbought means the price has risen quickly and may be due a pause or pullback. Oversold means it has fallen quickly and may be due a bounce. These are warnings, not guarantees: prices can keep going in the same direction.
entries.adult: Overbought/oversold readings (e.g. RSI above 70 / below 30) signal stretched short-term conditions. They are more reliable in range-bound markets; in trending markets they often just confirm strength or weakness.
entries.in_this_app: The RSI card tells you if the stock looks overbought or oversold right now.

entries.age_10: Imagine two runners: a quick one who reacts to the last few days, and a slower one who looks at a longer time. When the quick runner pulls ahead, the price is speeding up. When it falls behind, the price is slowing down.
entries.age_15: MACD compares a fast average (12-day) with a slow average (26-day) of the price. A 9-day average of MACD, called the signal line, is drawn too. MACD above the signal line suggests upward momentum; below it suggests downward momentum.
entries.adult: MACD = EMA(12) - EMA(26); signal = EMA(9) of MACD; histogram = MACD - signal. Crossovers indicate momentum shifts, and the zero line indicates whether the short-term average is above the long-term one. It's a lagging, trend-following momentum tool.
entries.in_this_app: The 'Momentum (MACD)' card says whether momentum is positive or negative right now.

entries.age_10: Momentum is like a ball rolling down a hill: once it's moving fast, it tends to keep going for a while. In stocks, prices that have been rising strongly often keep rising for a bit, and the same for falling.
entries.age_15: Momentum is how strongly and quickly a price is moving in one direction. Strong momentum suggests the move may continue; fading momentum can warn the trend is losing steam.
entries.adult: Momentum is one of the most documented market effects: assets that outperformed over recent months tend to keep outperforming over intermediate horizons, though momentum can reverse sharply. RSI and MACD are common momentum measures.
entries.in_this_app: RSI and MACD in 'Key signals' both measure momentum.

entries.age_10: Volatility is how bumpy the ride is. A calm stock is like a smooth road; a volatile stock is like a bumpy mountain road with big ups and downs.
entries.age_15: Volatility measures how much a price usually moves around. It's calculated from daily price changes and expressed per year. A stock with 30% volatility swings much more than one with 15%, so it is riskier but can also move up faster.
entries.adult: Annualised volatility = standard deviation of daily returns x the square root of 252 (trading days in a year). If returns followed a normal distribution, about two years in three would land within one volatility of the average. Real returns have fat tails, so big moves happen more often than that.
entries.in_this_app: The volatility card and the Risk and return section show this stock's yearly volatility.

entries.age_10: This tells you how much your money would have grown each year, on average, if you had bought the stock and kept it. A minus sign means it shrank.
entries.age_15: Average yearly return shows how much the investment grew per year, on average, over the chosen period. It smooths out good and bad years into one number.
entries.adult: Usually reported as CAGR: (ending value / starting value)^(1/years) - 1. It hides the path taken, so always read it alongside volatility and maximum drawdown.
entries.in_this_app: Shown in the Risk and return section, over 1, 3 or 5 years.

entries.age_10: Imagine your tower of blocks reaches its tallest, then falls down a bit. The worst fall is the biggest drop from the tallest point before it grew back. It shows the scariest moment an investor would have lived through.
entries.age_15: Maximum drawdown is the largest percentage drop from a peak to a later low during the period. A -30% drawdown means at the worst point, an investor would have been down 30% from the high.
entries.adult: Max drawdown captures the actual pain along the way, which volatility misses. It matters for real behaviour: deep drawdowns are where investors tend to panic-sell. Recovering from -50% requires a +100% gain.
entries.in_this_app: Shown as 'Worst fall (max drawdown)' in Risk and return, and for each strategy in Strategy tests.

entries.age_10: This answers: on a really bad day, how much could I lose? '1 day in 20' means if you watched for 20 days, roughly one of those days was at least this bad.
entries.age_15: VaR (95%) is the daily loss that was exceeded on only about 5% of days, or 1 day in 20, in the past. If VaR is 2%, then on about 1 day in 20 the stock fell 2% or more.
entries.adult: Historical 1-day VaR at 95% is the 5th percentile of daily returns. It doesn't say how bad losses beyond that level can be; for that, look at expected shortfall or max drawdown.
entries.in_this_app: Shown as 'Bad-day loss (VaR 95%)' in Risk and return.

entries.age_10: This is the money you could earn by keeping cash somewhere very safe, like lending to the government. A stock should earn more than this, because it's riskier.
entries.age_15: The risk-free rate is what you could earn with almost no risk, like a government bond. Ratios like Sharpe subtract it from the stock's return, to check whether taking risk actually paid off.
entries.adult: Typically proxied by government bond or treasury bill yields. It's the hurdle any risky investment should beat. Risk-adjusted ratios measure excess return over this rate.
entries.in_this_app: The app assumes a safe return of 6.5% a year, roughly an Indian government bond yield.

entries.age_10: Imagine two roads to school. One is fast but super bumpy, the other is a bit slower but smooth. The Sharpe ratio tells you how much 'getting there faster' you got for every bump. More reward for fewer bumps is better.
entries.age_15: The Sharpe ratio shows how much extra return you earned for each unit of risk (volatility), after subtracting the safe return. Above 1 is generally considered good. Below 0 means the stock didn't even beat the safe return.
entries.adult: Sharpe = (annual return - risk-free rate) / annualised volatility. It penalises upside and downside volatility equally and assumes roughly normal returns, so compare it alongside Sortino and drawdown.
entries.in_this_app: Shown in 'Reward for the risk taken' in the Risk and return section.

entries.age_10: Like the Sharpe ratio, but it only counts the bad bumps, the falls. Going up fast isn't scary, so it doesn't count that as risk.
entries.age_15: The Sortino ratio is like Sharpe but only treats downward swings as risk. Higher is better. It's fairer for stocks that jump up a lot, since big upward moves aren't 'bad' risk.
entries.adult: Sortino = (return - target or risk-free rate) / downside deviation. It distinguishes harmful volatility from beneficial upside volatility.
entries.in_this_app: Shown in 'Reward for the risk taken'.

entries.age_10: This compares how much the stock grew each year with its biggest scary fall. Growing a lot without big falls is best.
entries.age_15: The Calmar ratio is the yearly return divided by the maximum drawdown. It tells you how much growth you got for the worst pain you had to sit through. Higher is better.
entries.adult: Calmar = annualised return / size of the maximum drawdown. Popular with trend followers and fund analysts because it focuses on the worst loss rather than average volatility.
entries.in_this_app: Shown in 'Reward for the risk taken'.

entries.age_10: This checks how much extra money you got for riding along with the whole market's ups and downs.
entries.age_15: The Treynor ratio is the extra return above the safe rate divided by beta. It measures reward for market risk only, the part you can't get rid of by owning many stocks.
entries.adult: Treynor = (return - risk-free rate) / beta. Most meaningful for a diversified portfolio, where company-specific risk is diversified away and market (systematic) risk remains.
entries.in_this_app: Shown in 'Reward for the risk taken'.

entries.age_10: The Nifty 50 is like a class average. It combines 50 of India's biggest companies into one number, so you can see if the whole market went up or down, and compare one stock with everyone else.
entries.age_15: The Nifty 50 is an index of 50 large companies on the NSE. It's used as a benchmark: if your stock went up 10% but the Nifty went up 15%, your stock actually did worse than the market. The Sensex is a similar index of 30 companies on the BSE.
entries.adult: The Nifty 50 is weighted by free-float market capitalisation and is the standard Indian equity benchmark. Comparing a stock against it separates stock-specific performance from overall market moves.
entries.in_this_app: Beta, alpha, information ratio and correlation all compare the stock with the Nifty 50.

entries.age_10: If the whole market is a big wave, beta tells you if this stock is a big boat or a small boat. Beta 1 means it moves just like the wave. Beta 1.5 means it bounces more. Beta 0.5 means it's calmer.
entries.age_15: Beta measures how much a stock tends to move when the Nifty moves. A beta of 1.2 means that when the Nifty moves 1%, the stock has typically moved about 1.2%. Above 1 means more swing than the market; below 1 means less.
entries.adult: Beta = covariance of the stock's returns with the market's, divided by the variance of the market's returns. It measures sensitivity to market (systematic) risk and is estimated from history, so it can change over time.
entries.in_this_app: Shown in 'Compared with the Nifty 50'.

entries.age_10: Alpha is the extra marks you got beyond what was expected. If the class got easier questions and everyone scored high, alpha checks whether you did better than you 'should' have.
entries.age_15: Alpha is the return a stock earned beyond what its beta and the market's movement would predict. Positive alpha means it did better than expected for its risk; negative means worse.
entries.adult: Jensen's alpha = actual return - [risk-free rate + beta x (market return - risk-free rate)]. Positive alpha suggests stock-specific outperformance, though historical alpha often doesn't persist.
entries.in_this_app: Shown as 'Alpha (yearly)' in 'Compared with the Nifty 50'.

entries.age_10: This checks if the stock beat the market steadily, like getting slightly better marks than the class every single test, rather than one lucky high score.
entries.age_15: The information ratio measures how consistently a stock beat (or trailed) the Nifty, compared with how much its returns differed from the Nifty. Above 0.5 is generally considered good.
entries.adult: IR = (stock return - benchmark return) / tracking error. It rewards outperformance that is steady rather than lucky, and is widely used to judge active fund managers.
entries.in_this_app: Shown in 'Compared with the Nifty 50'.

entries.age_10: Correlation tells you if two things move together, like best friends who always walk side by side. 1 means they always move together, 0 means they don't care about each other, and below 0 means they go opposite ways.
entries.age_15: Correlation runs from -1 to +1 and shows how closely a stock's daily moves match the Nifty's. High correlation means it mostly follows the market; low correlation means it does its own thing.
entries.adult: Pearson correlation of daily returns. Low-correlation holdings improve diversification. Correlations tend to rise during market crises, exactly when diversification is needed most.
entries.in_this_app: Shown as 'Correlation with Nifty' in 'Compared with the Nifty 50'.

entries.age_10: Imagine rolling dice 2,000 times to guess where a toy car might end up after 30 days of random moves. Monte Carlo does that with a stock, using how bumpy it has been in the past. It doesn't tell you where the price WILL go, just where it COULD go.
entries.age_15: A Monte Carlo simulation creates thousands of possible future price paths using random daily moves based on the stock's past behaviour. Looking at where all the paths end shows a range of likely outcomes and their chances. It's a range of possibilities, not a forecast.
entries.adult: The model draws random daily returns based on historical volatility (and possibly drift) to build many price paths, then reads percentiles of the ending prices. Limits: it assumes the future resembles the past, ignores news and events, and normal-distribution models underestimate crash risk.
entries.in_this_app: The 'Possible outcomes' tab runs 2,000 simulated futures for 30, 60 or 90 days.

entries.age_10: The shaded fan shows where the price ended up in all those pretend futures. The darker the shade, the more futures landed there. The dotted line in the middle is the 'middle' result: half ended above it, half below.
entries.age_15: The '70% chance' range means 70% of the simulated futures ended between those two prices. The darkest band holds 50% of futures, then 70%, then 90%. The median is the middle result. Wider fans mean more uncertainty.
entries.adult: The bands are percentile ranges of the simulated ending prices (for example the 15th to 85th percentile for the 70% band). They describe uncertainty under the model's assumptions; real outcomes can and do fall outside them.
entries.in_this_app: Shown at the top of 'Possible outcomes' and in the price paths chart.

entries.age_10: This dial shows what share of the pretend futures ended higher than today. It's not a real promise. It just shows how the pretend futures turned out.
entries.age_15: It's the percentage of the simulated futures that finished above today's price. It depends completely on the simulation's assumptions, so it isn't real knowledge of what will happen. Around 50% means no clear lean either way.
entries.adult: This percentage is a direct product of the model's assumptions, especially whether the simulation includes the stock's past average direction (drift). If past drift is included, recent winners lean higher and recent losers lean lower, which isn't evidence about the future.
entries.in_this_app: The gauge in 'Possible outcomes'. This app does include the stock's past-year average direction in the simulation.

entries.age_10: A backtest is like replaying an old cricket match with a new plan, to see if your plan would have won. We take the last 5 years of prices and pretend we followed a rule, to see how it would have done.
entries.age_15: A backtest applies a trading rule to past prices to see how it would have performed, then compares it with simply buying and holding. Past results don't guarantee future results, but it shows how a rule behaves.
entries.adult: Backtests are prone to overfitting, look-ahead bias and survivorship bias, and must include costs. This one acts on signals the next day to avoid look-ahead bias and includes a trading cost per switch.
entries.in_this_app: The Strategy tests tab replays the last 5 years starting with Rs 1,00,000.

entries.age_10: Buy and hold means you buy a share and just keep it, no matter what happens, like planting a tree and leaving it to grow.
entries.age_15: Buy and hold means buying on day one and never selling. It's the simple benchmark every trading rule has to beat; many rules fail to beat it once costs are included.
entries.adult: Buy-and-hold captures the full market return with minimal costs and taxes. Active rules must beat it after costs to add value, often by reducing drawdowns rather than raising returns.
entries.in_this_app: Every strategy test is compared with buy and hold.

entries.age_10: The rule: own the stock while the 50-day line is above the 200-day line (things look good), and keep your money aside safely when it's below (things look bad).
entries.age_15: Hold the stock while its 50-day average is above its 200-day average, otherwise stay in cash. It aims to avoid long downtrends, but it reacts late and can get fooled when prices move sideways.
entries.adult: A classic trend-following filter. It typically reduces drawdowns but can lag buy-and-hold in strong rising markets and suffer whipsaws when prices move sideways.
entries.in_this_app: In Strategy tests and Possible outcomes.

entries.age_10: This rule buys when the RSI speedometer shows the price has fallen a lot (might bounce), and sells when it shows the price has recovered.
entries.age_15: A mean-reversion rule: buy when RSI shows the stock is oversold and sell once it has recovered. It works best when prices move sideways, and poorly in strong trends.
entries.adult: A counter-trend (mean-reversion) rule based on RSI thresholds. Such rules usually have a high win rate but small wins, and can suffer badly when a trend keeps going.
entries.in_this_app: In Strategy tests and Possible outcomes. Here it buys when the 14-day RSI falls below 30 and sells when it rises above 55.

entries.age_10: This rule owns the stock when the quick runner is ahead of the slow runner (price speeding up), and steps aside when it falls behind.
entries.age_15: A momentum rule based on MACD: typically holding the stock when MACD is above its signal line and moving to cash when it drops below. The exact rule is shown in the app.
entries.adult: A momentum/trend-following rule based on MACD signal crossovers. It responds faster than a 50/200 crossover but trades more often, so costs matter more.
entries.in_this_app: In Strategy tests and Possible outcomes.

entries.age_10: This rule buys when the price drops to the bottom edge of its usual road, hoping it bounces back to the middle, and sells when it gets back up.
entries.age_15: A mean-reversion rule using Bollinger Bands, typically buying near the lower band and selling near the middle or upper band. The exact rule is shown in the app.
entries.adult: A mean-reversion rule assuming the price returns to its 20-day average. It struggles in strong trends, where the price can 'walk the band'.
entries.in_this_app: In Strategy tests and Possible outcomes.

entries.age_10: Every time you buy or sell, you pay a small fee, like a delivery charge. If you buy and sell too often, all these small fees add up and eat your profit.
entries.age_15: Real trades carry costs: brokerage, Securities Transaction Tax (STT), exchange charges, GST and stamp duty. They're small per trade, but rules that trade often can lose their advantage because of them.
entries.adult: Trading costs plus slippage can turn a profitable-looking backtest into a losing one, especially for strategies that trade often. Capital gains tax further reduces realised gains.
entries.in_this_app: Strategy tests let you set a trading cost each time the rule switches (default 0.10%).

entries.term: Past results don't predict the future
entries.age_10: Just because you won a game yesterday doesn't mean you'll win tomorrow. Markets change, so a rule that worked before might not work next time.
entries.age_15: Backtests and simulations use old data. Markets change because of news, the economy and people's behaviour, so something that worked in the past can stop working.
entries.adult: Historical results can stop working when market conditions change, and rules can be overfitted to old data. Testing a rule on data it wasn't designed on reduces, but never removes, this risk.
entries.in_this_app: Every strategy and simulation section carries this warning.

entries.age_10: Technical analysis means studying the price chart, like reading footprints, to understand what buyers and sellers are doing and guess where things may head.
entries.age_15: Technical analysis studies price, trends, momentum and volume to understand market behaviour and timing. It assumes prices reflect what buyers and sellers think and that trends tend to persist.
entries.adult: TA studies market-generated data to assess supply and demand, trend, momentum and risk. Practitioners use it for timing, risk management (stops, position sizing) and relative-strength selection. The CMT designation certifies this discipline.
entries.in_this_app: Charts, Key signals and Strategy tests are technical analysis.

entries.age_10: Fundamental analysis is checking how healthy a company really is, like checking a lemonade stand's sales, profits and debts before deciding if it's a good business.
entries.age_15: Fundamental analysis studies a company's business and numbers, like sales, profits, debt and how expensive the share is compared with earnings, to judge what it is really worth.
entries.adult: FA evaluates financial statements, competitive position, management and valuation to estimate intrinsic value. It answers 'what to own'; it says little about timing.
entries.in_this_app: The Fusion analysis tab shows key fundamentals from Yahoo Finance.

entries.age_10: Fusion analysis is using two tools together: checking if the company is healthy (fundamentals) AND checking if its price is actually going up (technicals). It's like picking a good player who's also in good form right now.
entries.age_15: Fusion analysis combines fundamental and technical analysis. Fundamentals help decide what is worth owning; technicals help decide when. It's taught in the CMT Level 3 curriculum.
entries.adult: As taught in CMT Level 3 (David Lundgren, John Letizia): fundamentals identify candidates, while trend and momentum confirm, delay or reject timing. When they diverge, the emphasis shifts to risk management until they converge again.
entries.in_this_app: The Fusion analysis tab places each stock in the Winner's Circle.

entries.age_10: Picture three circles: 'price going up', 'healthy company' and 'good price to buy'. The best stocks sit in all three circles at once. The more circles a stock is in, the better it looks.
entries.age_15: From CMT Level 3 (David Lundgren): three overlapping circles, Trend & Momentum, Fundamentals and Valuation. A stock scores by how many circles it falls in. The key rule: avoid stocks outside the Trend & Momentum circle, however good the business looks.
entries.adult: Lundgren's framework ranks stocks by overlap of trend/momentum, fundamental quality and valuation. Trend & momentum is the gatekeeper, reflecting his view that 'the market is the best fundamental analyst on the planet.'
entries.in_this_app: The 'three circles' section of the Fusion analysis tab shows whether the chosen company is in each circle and which group (1 to 4) it falls in.

entries.age_10: Price depends on how good the company is and how fairly priced it is, but people's mood can make it go up or down much more. When everyone is happy, prices go extra high; when everyone is scared, even good companies get cheap.
entries.age_15: Lundgren's formula: Price = (Fundamentals x Value) raised to the power of Sentiment. In bull markets S is above 1, so mood pushes prices above what the business alone justifies. In bear markets S is below 1, pulling prices down. S = 1 is the rare calm state.
entries.adult: A conceptual model (not a calculator) showing sentiment acting as an exponent on fundamentals and valuation. It explains why strong companies can fall in bear markets and weak ones can soar in bull markets.
entries.in_this_app: Explained in the Fusion analysis tab.

entries.age_10: First you find a good company. Then you check the chart to see if now is a good time. If the chart says 'not yet', you wait.
entries.age_15: In the technical overlay approach (John Letizia, CMT Level 3), fundamentals decide what to consider and technicals confirm, delay or reject the timing. A good company in a downtrend is 'good company, poor timing'.
entries.adult: The overlay model keeps fundamentals as the primary selection driver while using trend, momentum and support/resistance for entry timing and risk control, reducing the chance of buying into a falling trend.
entries.in_this_app: The plain-English verdict in the Fusion analysis tab.

entries.age_10: Relative strength checks if a stock is running faster than the whole race. If the market goes up 5% but your stock goes up 10%, your stock is relatively strong.
entries.age_15: Relative strength compares a stock's performance with a benchmark like the Nifty 50, often by dividing the stock's price by the index. A rising line means the stock is beating the market. (It's different from RSI, despite the similar name.)
entries.adult: Relative strength as a price ratio (stock / index) can be analysed like any price chart, for example with a moving average on the ratio. It underpins sector rotation and momentum strategies.
entries.in_this_app: Used in the Trend & Momentum circle of fusion analysis (6-month return compared with the Nifty 50).

entries.age_10: Revenue is all the money a lemonade stand collects from selling lemonade, before paying for lemons, sugar and cups.
entries.age_15: Revenue is the total money a company earns from selling its products or services, before subtracting costs. Growing revenue usually means the business is expanding.
entries.adult: The top line of the income statement. Revenue growth shows demand; it should be read alongside margins, since growth at falling profitability can destroy value.
entries.in_this_app: Revenue growth is part of the Fundamentals circle.

entries.age_10: Net profit is what the lemonade stand keeps after paying for everything: lemons, cups, rent and taxes.
entries.age_15: Net profit is what's left after all costs, interest and taxes are paid. Divided by the number of shares, it gives earnings per share (EPS), used in the P/E ratio.
entries.adult: Profit after tax (PAT) is the bottom line. Look at growth and quality: earnings backed by operating cash flow are more reliable than one-off gains.
entries.in_this_app: Profit growth is part of the Fundamentals circle.

entries.age_10: If the owners put Rs 100 into the lemonade stand and it makes Rs 20 profit a year, that's an ROE of 20%. It shows how well the company uses its owners' money.
entries.age_15: ROE = net profit / shareholders' equity. It shows how much profit the company makes from the owners' money. Higher is generally better, often 15% or more is considered strong.
entries.adult: ROE measures profit relative to shareholders' equity. A high ROE driven mostly by heavy debt is lower quality, so always read it alongside debt-to-equity.
entries.in_this_app: Part of the Fundamentals circle.

entries.age_10: If you sell lemonade for Rs 10 and keep Rs 2 after costs, your margin is 20%. Bigger margins mean you keep more of every rupee you earn.
entries.age_15: Operating margin is profit from the main business divided by revenue; net margin is final profit divided by revenue. Higher, stable margins usually signal a strong business.
entries.adult: Margins reflect pricing power and cost efficiency. Compare within the same industry, since normal margins vary widely between sectors.
entries.in_this_app: Operating margin is part of the Fundamentals circle.

entries.age_10: This shows how much the company borrowed compared with the owners' own money. Borrowing too much is risky, like owing your friends more pocket money than you have.
entries.age_15: Debt-to-equity = total debt / shareholders' equity. A high number means the company relies heavily on borrowed money, which increases risk if business slows down.
entries.adult: Leverage magnifies returns and risk. Acceptable levels vary by sector (banks and utilities differ from software companies). Interest coverage shows whether earnings comfortably cover interest costs.
entries.in_this_app: Part of the Fundamentals circle (not used for banks and lenders, where debt is their business).

entries.age_10: P/E tells you how many years of profit you're paying for. If a lemonade stand makes Rs 10 a year and costs Rs 200, you're paying 20 years of profit. That's a P/E of 20.
entries.age_15: P/E = share price / earnings per share. A high P/E means investors pay a lot for each rupee of profit, often because they expect growth. A low P/E may mean cheap, or that the business has problems.
entries.adult: P/E is best compared with the company's own history, its sector and its growth rate (PEG). It's unreliable when earnings are temporarily depressed or negative.
entries.in_this_app: Part of the Valuation circle.

entries.age_10: Book value is what the company's stuff would be worth on paper if you added it all up and subtracted what it owes. P/B compares the share price with that number.
entries.age_15: P/B = share price / book value per share. A P/B of 1 means you pay about what the company's net assets are worth on paper. It's most useful for banks and businesses that own lots of buildings, machines or loans.
entries.adult: P/B is a key measure for banks and other financial companies, whose assets are mostly money. For companies whose value lies in brands, software or people, book value understates real worth, so P/B tells you less.
entries.in_this_app: Part of the Valuation circle.

entries.age_10: Valuation is asking: is this toy priced fairly, too high, or a bargain? Even the best toy is a bad buy if it costs way too much.
entries.age_15: Valuation judges whether a stock's price is reasonable compared with its earnings, assets or growth, using ratios like P/E and P/B. A great company can still be a poor investment if bought at too high a price.
entries.adult: Valuation is a poor short-term timing tool (expensive stocks can get more expensive), but it strongly influences long-term returns and downside risk.
entries.in_this_app: One of the three circles in fusion analysis.

entries.age_10: Sentiment is the market's mood. A bull market is when people are happy and prices keep going up. A bear market is when people are scared and prices keep falling.
entries.age_15: Sentiment is how optimistic or fearful investors feel. In bull markets, optimism pushes prices up; in bear markets, fear pushes them down. Mood can move prices far away from what businesses are really worth.
entries.adult: Sentiment drives deviations from fundamental value. Contrarians watch for extremes (euphoria at tops, capitulation at bottoms), while trend followers ride sentiment until price action shows it turning.
entries.in_this_app: Sentiment is the 'S' in the P = (F x V)^S formula in Fusion analysis.

entries.age_10: Don't put all your eggs in one basket. If you drop it, they all break. Owning different kinds of companies means one bad one won't ruin everything.
entries.age_15: Diversification means spreading money across different companies and sectors, so a problem in one doesn't hurt the whole portfolio too much. It reduces company-specific risk but not overall market risk.
entries.adult: Diversification reduces company-specific (unsystematic) risk, and works best when holdings have low correlation. Market (systematic) risk remains and can only be managed through asset allocation and hedging.
entries.in_this_app: Try buying stocks from different sectors in paper trading.

entries.age_10: A sector is a group of similar companies, like all the banks, or all the car makers. Companies in the same sector often move together.
entries.age_15: A sector groups companies doing similar business, such as banking, IT, pharma, auto or FMCG. Sector news, like interest rate changes for banks, can move all of them together.
entries.adult: Sector exposure drives a large share of stock returns. Sector rotation strategies put more money in sectors with strong relative strength and less in weak ones.
entries.in_this_app: Owning stocks from several sectors makes your paper portfolio more diversified.

entries.age_10: A dividend is like pocket money a company gives its owners from its profits, a little reward for owning its shares.
entries.age_15: A dividend is a part of a company's profit paid to shareholders, usually in cash. Dividend yield = yearly dividend / share price. Mature companies often pay more; fast-growing ones often reinvest instead.
entries.adult: Dividends contribute meaningfully to long-term total return. In India, dividends are taxable in the shareholder's hands. Total-return comparisons should include them.
entries.in_this_app: Paper trading doesn't add dividends to your balance.

entries.age_10: A split is like cutting a pizza into more slices. You have more slices, but each is smaller, so you still have the same amount of pizza.
entries.age_15: In a split or bonus issue, a company gives shareholders more shares, and the price per share drops in proportion. Your total value stays the same; only the number of shares changes.
entries.adult: Splits and bonuses are cosmetic for value but need price data to be adjusted; otherwise charts and returns show a false crash.
entries.in_this_app: Paper trading may not adjust automatically for splits, so a holding could look like it suddenly fell.

entries.age_10: Interest is the extra money you pay when you borrow, or get when you save. When interest rates change, it changes how people feel about spending and investing.
entries.age_15: Interest rates are the cost of borrowing money. In India the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) sets a key rate. Higher rates make loans costlier and safe savings more attractive, which can pull stock prices down; lower rates often help stocks.
entries.adult: Rates affect company borrowing costs, consumer demand, and how much investors are willing to pay today for future profits. Rate-sensitive sectors like banks, real estate and autos often react most.
entries.in_this_app: Not shown directly, but interest rates influence the safe return (risk-free rate) the app uses.

entries.age_10: Volume is how many shares changed hands in a day, like counting how many people bought tickets at a cinema. A big crowd means lots of interest.
entries.age_15: Volume is the number of shares traded in a period. Price moves on high volume are taken more seriously than moves on low volume, because more people took part.
entries.adult: Volume confirms price moves: breakouts on rising volume are more reliable, and falling volume during a trend can warn of fading participation.
entries.in_this_app: The current app charts price only, not volume.

entries.age_10: Market cap is the price of the whole company: the price of one share times all the shares. It tells you how big a company is.
entries.age_15: Market cap = share price x total number of shares. Companies are called large-cap, mid-cap or small-cap by size. Free float counts only shares easily available for trading, not those held by the company's promoters (founders and controlling owners).
entries.adult: Market cap reflects the equity value the market assigns. Indices like the Nifty 50 weight companies by free-float market cap, so the biggest companies move the index most.
entries.in_this_app: The Nifty 50 used for comparison is weighted by free-float market cap.

entries.age_10: A broker is like a shopkeeper who lets you buy shares from the stock market. You can't walk into the NSE yourself, so the broker does it for you.
entries.age_15: A broker is a SEBI-registered company that places your buy and sell orders on the exchange. Today most brokers work through apps and websites, and charge a fee called brokerage.
entries.adult: Brokers provide market access, a trading account linked to your demat account, and order execution. Charges and service quality vary, so compare them.
entries.in_this_app: This app isn't a broker. No real orders are placed.

entries.age_10: SEBI is like the referee of India's stock market. It makes the rules and makes sure people play fairly.
entries.age_15: SEBI (Securities and Exchange Board of India) regulates India's stock markets, brokers, mutual funds and investment advisers, to protect investors. A SEBI-registered investment adviser is licensed to give personal financial advice.
entries.adult: SEBI oversees exchanges, brokers and other market firms, company disclosures and market conduct. Only SEBI-registered investment advisers and research analysts may legally give paid investment advice or recommendations.
entries.in_this_app: The app gives no advice; for personal advice, consult a SEBI-registered investment adviser.

entries.term: Demat account, KYC, PAN and Aadhaar
entries.age_10: To own real shares you need a special account, like a locker where your shares are kept safely. To open it, you show ID cards so they know who you are.
entries.age_15: A demat account holds your shares electronically; a trading account lets you buy and sell. To open them you complete KYC ('Know Your Customer') using your PAN card, Aadhaar and bank details.
entries.adult: Demat accounts are held with depositories (NSDL or CDSL) through a depository participant, usually your broker. KYC is mandatory under SEBI rules.
entries.in_this_app: Not needed for this app. It only uses virtual money.

entries.age_10: An index fund is like buying a tiny bit of every company in a big group, like the Nifty 50, all at once, instead of picking just one.
entries.age_15: An index fund (or ETF) copies an index such as the Nifty 50, so your money is spread across all its companies. It's simple, diversified and usually cheap, but it can't beat the index it follows.
entries.adult: Passive index funds deliver the market return minus low fees. Over long periods, most active funds fail to beat their benchmark after costs, which is why index funds are popular core holdings.
entries.in_this_app: Paper trading includes a list of ETFs, which you can buy like shares. Buy-and-hold of the Nifty 50 is similar to owning an index fund.

entries.age_10: Liquidity is how easy it is to swap something for money quickly. A popular toy sells instantly; a strange one might take ages to find a buyer.
entries.age_15: A liquid stock trades a lot, so you can buy or sell quickly at a fair price. Illiquid stocks trade rarely, so prices can jump and selling can be hard.
entries.adult: Liquidity shows up as high volume and narrow bid-ask spreads. Low liquidity raises trading costs and slippage, especially in small companies.
entries.in_this_app: Large Nifty companies in the app are generally very liquid.

entries.age_10: A market order means 'buy it now at whatever the price is right now'. It's fast, but you don't choose the exact price.
entries.age_15: A market order buys or sells immediately at the best available price. A limit order only trades at the price you set or better, but may not happen at all.
entries.adult: Market orders guarantee execution but not price; limit orders guarantee price but not execution. In fast or illiquid markets, market orders can suffer slippage.
entries.in_this_app: Paper trades in the app work like market orders at the latest price.

entries.age_10: A shop buys old toys from you for Rs 90 and sells them for Rs 100. That Rs 10 gap is like the spread. Buyers and sellers in the market have a small gap too.
entries.age_15: The bid is the highest price buyers are offering; the ask is the lowest price sellers want. The gap between them is the spread. Every quick buy-then-sell loses roughly this gap.
entries.adult: The spread is an implicit trading cost, small for liquid large-caps and wider for illiquid stocks. Market makers and active traders earn it.
entries.in_this_app: Paper trading ignores the spread and uses one price.

entries.age_10: Slippage is when you plan to buy at one price but end up paying a little more because the price moved while your order was going through.
entries.age_15: Slippage is the difference between the price you expected and the price you actually got. It happens in fast-moving or thinly traded stocks.
entries.adult: Slippage is a hidden trading cost that backtests often underestimate. It grows with order size, volatility and low liquidity.
entries.in_this_app: The app's strategy tests don't model slippage, only a fixed trading cost.

entries.age_10: When you sell something for more than you paid, the government takes a small part of your profit as tax.
entries.age_15: Capital gains tax is tax on profit from selling investments. In India, rates differ for short-term gains (shares held up to a year) and long-term gains. Exact rates change with government budgets.
entries.adult: Indian listed equity gains are split into short-term (held 12 months or less) and long-term, taxed at different rates with an exemption limit for long-term gains. Check current rules, as they change.
entries.in_this_app: Paper trading and backtests in the app don't include tax.

entries.age_10: A government bond is like lending money to the government. It promises to pay you back with a little extra. Because governments rarely fail to pay, it's very safe.
entries.age_15: A bond is a loan you give, and you get regular interest. Government bonds are among the safest investments. Yield is the yearly return you get on a bond at its current price.
entries.adult: Government securities (G-Secs and T-bills) set the baseline risk-free return. Rising yields raise the hurdle for stocks and usually weigh on valuations.
entries.in_this_app: The app's 6.5% safe return is roughly an Indian government bond yield.

entries.age_10: A position is how much of one stock you own. Position sizing is deciding how much to buy, so one bad pick can't hurt you too much.
entries.age_15: Your position is the shares you hold in one stock. Position sizing means choosing how much money to put in, often based on how much you're willing to lose if it goes wrong.
entries.adult: Common methods size each position so that the loss if the stop-loss is hit equals a small fixed share of capital (for example 1%), or put less money into more volatile stocks.
entries.in_this_app: In paper trading, try not to put all your money in one stock.

entries.age_10: A stop-loss is a promise to yourself: 'If the price falls to this level, I'll sell so I don't lose too much.' It's like a seatbelt.
entries.age_15: A stop-loss is a preset price where you sell to limit a loss. Technicians often place it just below a support level.
entries.adult: Stops turn an open-ended risk into a defined one and are the basis of position sizing. Too tight and normal noise triggers them; too wide and losses grow.
entries.in_this_app: Not built into the app's paper trading.

entries.age_10: An investor plants a tree and waits years for it to grow. A trader buys and sells fruit at the market every day, trying to make small quick profits.
entries.age_15: Investors usually hold for years, focusing on the business. Traders hold for days or weeks, focusing more on price movements and timing. Trading costs more and is harder to do well.
entries.adult: The distinction is mostly about holding period and decision drivers. Most retail traders underperform after costs; long-term investing benefits from compounding and lower taxes.
entries.in_this_app: The app supports both styles: analysis for investors, signals and strategy tests for traders.

entries.age_10: Return is how much your money grows. Risk is how much it might shrink or jump around on the way. Usually, the chance of bigger rewards comes with bigger risks.
entries.age_15: Return is the gain or loss on an investment. Risk is the uncertainty, including the chance of losing money. Higher potential returns usually come with higher risk, which is why ratios like Sharpe compare the two.
entries.adult: Risk is measured by volatility, drawdown, VaR and beta; return by CAGR or total return. Good investing is about return per unit of risk, not return alone.
entries.in_this_app: The Risk and return section shows both side by side.

entries.age_10: A price target is a guess about where the price might reach, like guessing how high a ball will bounce. It's only a guess.
entries.age_15: A price target is an estimated level a price could reach. Technicians calculate them from chart patterns (like measured moves); analysts calculate them from company valuations.
entries.adult: Technical targets come from pattern height, measured moves or Fibonacci extensions; fundamental targets from valuation models. Both are estimates, best used for risk/reward planning.
entries.in_this_app: The app doesn't give price targets. Its simulation shows a range instead.

entries.age_10: Trend following is like surfing: you wait for a wave to start, ride it as long as it lasts, and get off when it ends.
entries.age_15: Trend following means buying things that are going up and selling when the trend breaks, instead of guessing tops and bottoms. It accepts many small losses to catch a few big winners.
entries.adult: Trend-following systems have low win rates but large average wins (a 'fat right tail'), and must tolerate drawdowns. Moving-average and breakout rules are typical.
entries.in_this_app: The moving-average crossover and MACD rules in Strategy tests are trend-following rules.

entries.age_10: Mean reversion is like a stretched rubber band: if the price stretches too far from normal, it often snaps back towards the middle.
entries.age_15: Mean reversion is the idea that prices that move far from their average tend to come back. Counter-trend rules buy after big falls and sell after big rises.
entries.adult: Counter-trend strategies have high win rates with smaller gains, and the risk of large losses when a move keeps going. They suit sideways markets.
entries.in_this_app: The RSI and Bollinger Bands rules in Strategy tests are mean-reversion rules.

entries.age_10: A whipsaw is when a signal says 'go!' and then right away says 'stop!', so you buy and then quickly have to sell, losing a bit each time.
entries.age_15: A whipsaw happens when a price moves one way, triggers a signal, then quickly reverses. It's common when prices move sideways, and it makes trading rules lose money through repeated small losses and costs.
entries.adult: Whipsaws are the main cost of trend-following filters in range-bound markets. Filters like confirmation periods reduce them but add lag.
entries.in_this_app: Visible in Strategy tests as frequent buy/sell switches.

entries.age_10: A lagging indicator is like hearing thunder after the lightning: it tells you what already happened, a little late.
entries.age_15: Lagging indicators, like moving averages, confirm a trend only after it has started, so their signals come late. Leading indicators try to warn earlier but give more false signals.
entries.adult: Most trend indicators lag by construction because they average past prices. The trade-off is reliability versus speed.
entries.in_this_app: Moving averages and MACD in the app are lagging indicators.

entries.age_10: Divergence is when the price says one thing but the speedometer (like RSI) says another, a hint that the price may be getting tired.
entries.age_15: A divergence happens when price makes a new high but an indicator like RSI makes a lower high (negative divergence), or price makes a new low while RSI makes a higher low (positive divergence). It can warn a trend is weakening.
entries.adult: Divergences signal weakening momentum, not reversal timing. They can persist for long periods and work best with confirmation from price.
entries.in_this_app: Indicator-versus-price divergence isn't flagged automatically. (The Fusion tab has a separate flag for when the business and the price disagree.)

entries.age_10: An EMA is a moving average that listens more to the newest days, like a teacher who counts your latest test more than old ones.
entries.age_15: An EMA gives more weight to recent prices than a simple moving average, so it reacts faster to changes. MACD is built from EMAs.
entries.adult: The EMA weights prices with a factor of 2/(N+1), declining exponentially for older data. It reduces lag compared with an SMA but responds more to noise.
entries.in_this_app: MACD in the app uses 12- and 26-day EMAs.

entries.age_10: Standard deviation tells you how spread out things are. If your marks are always close to 80, it's small. If they jump between 40 and 100, it's big.
entries.age_15: Standard deviation measures how far values usually are from their average. In finance it measures how much returns vary, which is the basis of volatility and Bollinger Bands.
entries.adult: Standard deviation is the square root of variance. Applied to returns it measures dispersion; it treats up and down moves equally and assumes symmetric behaviour.
entries.in_this_app: Used for volatility and the width of Bollinger Bands (2 standard deviations).

entries.age_10: Most kids in a class are of average height, with only a few very short or very tall. Drawn as a picture, that looks like a bell. Stock markets are a bit different: really big jumps happen more often than the bell shape expects.
entries.age_15: A normal distribution is the bell-shaped curve where most values sit near the average. Many financial models assume returns follow it, but real markets have 'fat tails', meaning big crashes and jumps happen more often than the bell curve predicts.
entries.adult: Equity returns show excess kurtosis (fat tails) and often negative skew. Models assuming normality underestimate extreme-loss probability, which is why drawdown and VaR are reported alongside volatility.
entries.in_this_app: The simulation's limits section warns about this.

entries.age_10: Drift is which way the price has been leaning on average, like a boat slowly drifting with the current.
entries.age_15: In a simulation, drift is the average daily direction the price is assumed to move. Using past drift means a stock that rose will be simulated to keep rising, and vice versa, which isn't real knowledge of the future.
entries.adult: Historical drift is a noisy, unreliable estimate of expected return. Many practitioners set drift to zero or the risk-free rate and simulate only volatility.
entries.in_this_app: The app's simulation does use the stock's past-year average direction, which affects the 'chance of ending higher'.

entries.age_10: Variance measures how much something jumps around. Covariance checks whether two things jump around together.
entries.age_15: Variance is the square of the standard deviation, a measure of how spread out returns are. Covariance measures whether two investments tend to move in the same direction at the same time.
entries.adult: Covariance = correlation x the two standard deviations. Beta is the stock's covariance with the market divided by the market's variance.
entries.in_this_app: Used behind the scenes to calculate beta.

entries.age_10: Some risks hit everyone, like heavy rain on a picnic: that's market risk. Other risks hit only one person, like one kid dropping their sandwich: that's company-specific risk.
entries.age_15: Market (systematic) risk affects nearly all stocks, from things like recessions or interest rates. Company-specific (unsystematic) risk affects one company, like a bad product. Owning many stocks reduces company risk, but not market risk.
entries.adult: Diversification eliminates most unsystematic risk; systematic risk is what beta measures and what investors are paid for bearing, according to standard finance theory (CAPM).
entries.in_this_app: Beta and the Treynor ratio in the app focus on market risk.

entries.age_10: Tracking error shows how differently a stock moves compared with the market, like checking how far a kid strays from the group on a walk.
entries.age_15: Tracking error is how much a stock's or fund's returns differ from its benchmark over time. A small number means it closely follows the Nifty; a large one means it often goes its own way.
entries.adult: Tracking error = standard deviation of (portfolio return - benchmark return). It is the denominator of the information ratio.
entries.in_this_app: Used inside the information ratio.

entries.age_10: VaR tells you how bad a 'bad day' usually is. Expected shortfall asks: on the really, really bad days, how bad was it on average?
entries.age_15: Expected shortfall is the average loss on the worst days beyond the VaR level, for example the average of the worst 5% of days. It shows how deep the bad tail goes.
entries.adult: Expected shortfall (also called CVaR) captures how severe the worst losses are, which VaR ignores. Regulators increasingly prefer it.
entries.in_this_app: Not shown in the app; VaR is shown instead.

entries.term: Active vs passive investing / fund managers
entries.age_10: Active investing is like a coach picking the best players. Passive investing is just taking the whole team. A fund manager is the coach who picks for many people together.
entries.age_15: Active investing means choosing stocks to try to beat the market; passive means buying the whole index. Mutual funds pool money from many people, and fund managers invest it.
entries.adult: Active managers aim for alpha but charge higher fees; most fail to beat their benchmark over long periods after costs. Ratios like Sharpe and information ratio are used to evaluate them.
entries.in_this_app: The ratios in the app are the same ones used to judge fund managers.

entries.age_10: Overfitting is like memorising last year's exam answers. You'd score perfectly on that exact paper, but fail a new one.
entries.age_15: Overfitting means tweaking a strategy so much that it fits past data perfectly but fails in the future, because it learned random noise instead of a real pattern.
entries.adult: Overfitting rises with the number of parameters and tests tried. Defences include simple rules, testing on unseen data, and checking that results hold across many stocks and periods.
entries.in_this_app: The app uses standard, simple settings to reduce this risk.

entries.age_10: Look-ahead bias is like peeking at tomorrow's newspaper. A test that 'knows' the future will look amazing but isn't fair.
entries.age_15: Look-ahead bias happens when a backtest accidentally uses information that wasn't available at the time, like trading at today's close on a signal that only appears at today's close.
entries.adult: A common fix is acting on signals on the next day. Also watch for data that gets corrected later, such as company results that are revised.
entries.in_this_app: The app's strategy tests act on signals the next day to avoid this.

entries.age_10: If you only interview people who won the lottery, you'd think everyone wins. Survivorship bias is only looking at the winners who are still around.
entries.age_15: Survivorship bias happens when a study only includes companies that still exist today, ignoring the ones that failed or were removed. This makes past results look better than they really were.
entries.adult: Index constituents today exclude past failures; testing on today's list overstates historical returns. Proper tests use historical constituent lists.
entries.in_this_app: The app's companies are today's popular stocks, so long-term results may look rosier than reality.

entries.age_10: Intrinsic value is what something is really worth, not just what someone is asking for it today.
entries.age_15: Intrinsic value is an estimate of what a company is truly worth, based on its future profits and cash. If the share price is below it, value investors think the stock is cheap.
entries.adult: Typically estimated with discounted cash flow or relative valuation models. Estimates depend heavily on assumptions, so different analysts reach very different values.
entries.in_this_app: The app uses P/E and P/B as simple valuation checks instead.

entries.age_10: PEG checks if a fast-growing company is worth its high price. A high price is fine if the company is growing really fast.
entries.age_15: PEG = P/E ratio / earnings growth rate. It adjusts P/E for growth: a PEG around 1 is often seen as fair, below 1 as possibly cheap for its growth.
entries.adult: PEG is sensitive to the growth estimate used and is meaningless for low or negative growth.
entries.in_this_app: Not shown in the app.

entries.age_10: Interest coverage checks if a company earns enough to easily pay the interest on its loans, like checking your pocket money covers what you owe friends.
entries.age_15: Interest coverage = operating profit / interest expense. A higher number means the company can comfortably pay interest on its debt; below about 1.5 is a warning sign.
entries.adult: A key measure of whether a company can survive its debts (solvency), alongside debt-to-equity, especially for businesses whose profits rise and fall with the economy.
entries.in_this_app: Not used in the app; debt-to-equity is used instead.

entries.age_10: Cash flow is the real money coming into and going out of a business, like checking what's actually in the lemonade stand's money box.
entries.age_15: Cash flow is the actual cash a business generates. Operating cash flow comes from its main business; free cash flow is what remains after spending on things like machines and buildings.
entries.adult: Profits can be shaped by accounting choices; cash flow is harder to manipulate. Earnings consistently backed by operating cash flow are higher quality.
entries.in_this_app: Cash flow isn't used directly in the app's fusion scores.

entries.age_10: Financial statements are a company's report card. They show how much it earned, what it owns, what it owes, and where its cash went.
entries.age_15: Companies publish three main statements: the income statement (revenue and profit), the balance sheet (what it owns and owes) and the cash flow statement (cash in and out). Listed companies in India report results every quarter.
entries.adult: Analysts use these to compute growth, margins, returns on capital, leverage and cash conversion, and to compare companies across time and sectors.
entries.in_this_app: The Fusion analysis tab pulls key numbers from these statements via Yahoo Finance.

entries.age_10: Shareholders' equity is what the company would have left for its owners if it sold everything it owns and paid back everything it owes.
entries.age_15: Shareholders' equity = total assets - total liabilities. It's the owners' share of the company on paper, also called net worth or book value.
entries.adult: Shareholders' equity is the denominator for ROE and P/B. It can be distorted by accounting choices and one-off losses.
entries.in_this_app: Used in ROE, debt-to-equity and P/B.

entries.age_10: A contrarian does the opposite of the crowd, like going to the beach when everyone else is leaving, when it's quieter and cheaper.
entries.age_15: Contrarians buy when most people are scared and selling, and sell when most people are excited and buying, betting that crowds overreact at extremes.
entries.adult: Contrarian strategies exploit sentiment extremes but can underperform for long stretches; timing is hard, so many wait for price confirmation.
entries.in_this_app: Not a feature of the app, but sentiment ideas appear in Fusion analysis.

entries.age_10: Hedging is like carrying an umbrella. You hope it won't rain, but if it does, you're protected.
entries.age_15: Hedging means making an extra investment that gains when your main investment loses, to reduce risk. It costs something, like an insurance premium.
entries.adult: Common hedges include index options and futures, or holding assets that move differently from your main holdings. Hedging trades away some upside for protection.
entries.in_this_app: The app has no automatic hedging tool, but you can experiment with a short future or a put option in paper trading.

entries.age_10: Sector rotation is like switching to the team that's winning this season. Money moves towards sectors doing well and away from those doing badly.
entries.age_15: Sector rotation means shifting money between sectors (like IT, banks or pharma) based on which ones are strongest. 'Overweight' means owning more of a sector than the index; 'underweight' means less.
entries.adult: Usually driven by relative strength and economic-cycle views. As covered in CMT Level 3, rules often rebalance monthly using relative-strength trends.
entries.in_this_app: Not built in, but relative strength vs Nifty is the core ingredient.

entries.age_10: Risk management is making sure one mistake can't ruin you, like wearing knee pads when skating.
entries.age_15: Risk management means controlling how much you can lose: using stop-losses, sensible position sizes, diversification and not investing money you can't afford to lose.
entries.adult: In CMT terms, it covers position sizing, stop placement, drawdown control and correlation management. Many professionals consider it more important than picking entries.
entries.in_this_app: The risk measures in the app help you see how much risk a stock carries.

entries.age_10: Win rate is how often you win. But winning often isn't everything. Winning small and losing big can still lose overall.
entries.age_15: Win rate is the percentage of trades that make money. Expectancy combines it with the size of wins and losses: (win rate x average win) - (loss rate x average loss). Positive expectancy means a rule makes money on average.
entries.adult: Trend-following rules often win under 40% of the time but profit from big winners; counter-trend rules win often but risk large losses. Expectancy, not win rate, decides profitability.
entries.in_this_app: Strategy tests show the win rate, average win, average loss and expectancy per trade for each rule.

entries.age_10: Asset allocation is deciding how to split your money, like splitting pocket money between spending, saving and a piggy bank.
entries.age_15: Asset allocation means dividing money between different types of investments, like stocks, bonds, gold and cash. It decides much of how risky your overall investments are.
entries.adult: Strategic allocation sets long-term weights; tactical allocation adjusts them for market conditions. Allocation drives most of a portfolio's long-term risk profile.
entries.in_this_app: Paper trading lets you mix stocks, ETFs, bonds, futures and options, and the portfolio builder shows how your money is split.

entries.age_10: Algo trading is when a computer follows a set of rules to buy and sell, like a robot that never gets tired or emotional.
entries.age_15: Algorithmic trading uses computer programs to trade according to fixed rules. Quantitative (quant) trading designs those rules using statistics and data.
entries.adult: Covers strategy research, backtesting, execution and risk control. Programs like EPAT teach it, typically using Python.
entries.in_this_app: The strategy tests in the app are simple versions of rule-based (algorithmic) strategies.

entries.age_10: Python is a language for giving instructions to computers. This whole app is written in it.
entries.age_15: Python is a popular programming language, widely used in finance and data science. This app uses Python with libraries like Streamlit (for the website) and yfinance (for stock data).
entries.adult: Python dominates quantitative finance thanks to libraries such as pandas, NumPy and plotting tools. Streamlit turns Python scripts into web apps.
entries.in_this_app: The app is built in Python with Streamlit, yfinance, pandas and Plotly.

entries.age_10: An AI coding tool is a computer helper that can write code when you explain what you want, a bit like a very fast assistant.
entries.age_15: An AI coding tool writes and fixes code based on instructions. The student designed the features, chose the finance methods and checked the results, while the tool helped write the code.
entries.adult: AI-assisted development speeds up building, but the design, financial methodology and validation still need human expertise, which is where the CMT and EPAT knowledge came in.
entries.in_this_app: This app was coded with help from an AI coding tool. (This chat assistant is not AI: it only looks up written notes.)

entries.age_10: Compounding is when your money earns money, and then that extra money earns even more, like a snowball rolling downhill and getting bigger and bigger.
entries.age_15: Compounding means earning returns on your past returns. Rs 100 growing 10% a year becomes Rs 110, then Rs 121, then about Rs 133, and the growth speeds up over time. That's why starting early matters.
entries.adult: Compounding makes long holding periods powerful, and also why losses and high costs hurt so much: they shrink the base that future returns build on.
entries.in_this_app: Average yearly return in the app is a compounded yearly rate.

entries.age_10: Promoters are the people or family who started the company or control it, like the owner of the lemonade stand who invited friends to buy small parts.
entries.age_15: In India, promoters are the founders or controlling owners of a company. They usually hold a large share of it, and investors watch whether they are buying or selling their shares.
entries.adult: Promoter holding is closely watched in Indian markets; promoters borrowing against their own shares can be a warning sign. Shares held by promoters are excluded from free float.
entries.in_this_app: Not shown in the app.

entries.age_10: Options and futures are special agreements about buying or selling something later at a price agreed today, a bit like booking a toy now to buy next month.
entries.age_15: Futures are contracts to buy or sell at a fixed price on a future date. Options give the right, but not the duty, to buy (call) or sell (put) at a set price. They're used for hedging and speculation and can be very risky for beginners.
entries.adult: Derivatives allow leverage and hedging. In India, SEBI studies have found that most individual traders in futures and options lose money.
entries.in_this_app: Paper trading has Futures and Options tabs. Prices there are modelled (futures from the spot price and the safe rate, options with the Black-Scholes formula), not real NSE F&O prices, and you can only buy options.

entries.age_10: If lots of kids want a new toy and there are only a few, the price goes up. If nobody wants it, the price drops. Stock prices work the same way.
entries.age_15: Prices move because of supply (sellers) and demand (buyers). More eager buyers push prices up; more eager sellers push them down. Support and resistance are really levels of demand and supply.
entries.adult: Technical analysis reads supply and demand from price and volume. As CMT Level 3 notes, 'supply and demand' explains support and resistance more clearly to non-technicians.
entries.in_this_app: Every price move on the app's charts reflects supply and demand.

entries.age_10: The economy is like the weather for businesses. Sometimes it's sunny and everyone sells a lot; sometimes it's stormy (a recession) and sales drop for most companies.
entries.age_15: A recession is a period when the economy shrinks, businesses sell less and jobs are lost. Economies move in cycles of growth and slowdown. 'Cyclical' companies, like car makers, rise and fall more with these cycles.
entries.adult: Stock markets often fall before recessions begin and recover before they end, because prices discount expected future profits. Cyclical sectors are most sensitive; defensive sectors less so.
